{{Short description|Subset whose closure is the whole space}}{{Refimprove|date=February 2010}}

In [[topology]] and related areas of [[mathematics]], a [[subset]] ''A'' of a [[topological space]] ''X'' is said to be '''dense''' in ''X'' if every point of ''X'' either belongs to ''A'' or else is arbitrarily "close" to members of ''A'' &mdash; for instance, the [[rational number]]s are a dense subset of the [[real number]]s because every real number either is a rational number or has a rational number arbitrarily close to it (see [[Diophantine approximation]]). 
Formally, <math>A</math> is dense in <math>X</math> if the smallest [[Closed set|closed subset]] of <math>X</math> containing <math>A</math> is <math>X</math> itself.<ref name="CEIT">{{Citation|last=Steen|first=L. A.|last2=Seebach|first2=J. A.|title=Counterexamples in Topology|publisher=Dover|year=1995|isbn=0-486-68735-X|title-link=Counterexamples in Topology}}</ref> 

The '''{{visible anchor|density}}''' of a topological space <math>X</math> is the least [[cardinality]] of a dense subset of <math>X.</math>

==Definition==

A subset <math>A</math> of a [[topological space]] <math>X</math> is said to be a '''{{visible anchor|dense subset}} of <math>X</math>''' if any of the following equivalent conditions are satisfied:
<ol>
<li>The smallest [[Closed set|closed subset]] of <math>X</math> containing <math>A</math> is <math>X</math> itself.</li>
<li>The [[Closure (topology)|closure]] of <math>A</math> in <math>X</math> is equal to <math>X.</math> That is, <math>\operatorname{cl}_X A = X.</math></li>
<li>The [[Interior (topology)|interior]] of the [[complement (set theory)|complement]] of <math>A</math> is empty. That is, <math>\operatorname{int}_X (X \setminus A) = \varnothing.</math></li>
<li>Every point in <math>X</math> either belongs to <math>A</math> or is a [[limit point]] of <math>A.</math></li>
<li>For every <math>x \in X,</math> every [[Neighbourhood (mathematics)|neighborhood]] <math>U</math> of <math>x</math> [[Intersection (set theory)|intersects]] <math>A;</math> that is, <math>U \cap A \neq \varnothing.</math></li>
<li><math>A</math> intersects every non-empty open subset of <math>X.</math></li>
<li></li>
</ol>

and if <math>\mathcal{B}</math> is a [[Basis (topology)|basis]] of open sets for the topology on <math>X</math> then this list can be extended to include:
<ol start=7>
<li>For every <math>x \in X,</math> every {{em|basic}} [[Neighbourhood (mathematics)|neighborhood]] <math>B \in \mathcal{B}</math> of <math>x</math> [[Intersection (set theory)|intersects]] <math>A.</math></li>
<li><math>A</math> intersects every non-empty <math>B \in \mathcal{B}.</math></li>
</ol>

===Density in metric spaces===

An alternative definition of dense set in the case of [[metric space]]s is the following. When the [[Topology (structure)|topology]] of <math>X</math> is given by a [[Metric (mathematics)|metric]], the [[Topological closure|closure]] <math>\overline{A}</math> of <math>A</math> in <math>X</math> is the [[Union (set theory)|union]] of <math>A</math> and the set of all [[Limit of a sequence#Topological spaces|limits of sequences]] of elements in <math>A</math> (its ''limit points''),
<math display=block>\overline{A} = A \cup \left\{\lim_{n \to \infty} a_n : a_n \in A \text{ for all } n \in \N\right\}</math>

Then <math>A</math> is dense in <math>X</math> if 
<math display=block>\overline{A} = X.</math>

If <math>\left\{U_n\right\}</math> is a sequence of dense [[Open set|open]] sets in a complete metric space, <math>X,</math> then <math display=inline>\bigcap^{\infty}_{n=1} U_n</math> is also dense in <math>X.</math>  This fact is one of the equivalent forms of the [[Baire category theorem]].

==Examples==

The [[real number]]s with the usual topology have the [[rational number]]s as a [[Countable set|countable]] dense subset which shows that the [[cardinality]] of a dense subset of a topological space may be strictly smaller than the cardinality of the space itself. The [[irrational number]]s are another dense subset which shows that a topological space may have several [[Disjoint sets|disjoint]] dense subsets (in particular, two dense subsets may be each other's complements), and they need not even be of the same cardinality. Perhaps even more surprisingly, both the rationals and the irrationals have empty interiors, showing that dense sets need not contain any non-empty open set. The intersection of two dense open subsets of a topological space is again dense and open.<ref group=proof>Suppose that <math>A</math> and <math>B</math> are dense open subsets of a topological space <math>X.</math> If <math>X = \varnothing</math> then the conclusion that the open set <math>A \cap B</math> is dense in <math>X</math> is immediate, so assume otherwise. Let <math>U</math> is a non-empty open subset of <math>X,</math> so it remains to show that <math>U \cap (A \cap B)</math> is also not empty. Because <math>A</math> is dense in <math>X</math> and <math>U</math> is a non-empty open subset of <math>X,</math> their intersection <math>U \cap A</math> is not empty. Similarly, because <math>U \cap A</math> is a non-empty open subset of <math>X</math> and <math>B</math> is dense in <math>X,</math> their intersection <math>U \cap A \cap B</math> is not empty. <math>\blacksquare</math></ref> 
The [[empty set]] is a dense subset of itself. But every dense subset of a non-empty space must also be non-empty. 

By the [[Weierstrass approximation theorem]], any given [[Complex number|complex-valued]] [[continuous function]] defined on a [[closed interval]] <math>[a, b]</math> can be [[uniform convergence|uniformly approximated]] as closely as desired by a [[polynomial function]]. In other words, the polynomial functions are dense in the space <math>C[a, b]</math> of continuous complex-valued functions on the interval <math>[a, b],</math> equipped with the [[supremum norm]].

Every [[metric space]] is dense in its [[Completion (metric space)|completion]].

== Properties ==

Every [[topological space]] is a dense subset of itself. For a set <math>X</math> equipped with the [[discrete topology]], the whole space is the only dense subset. Every non-empty subset of a set <math>X</math> equipped with the [[trivial topology]] is dense, and every topology for which every non-empty subset is dense must be trivial.

Denseness is [[Transitive relation|transitive]]: Given three subsets <math>A, B</math> and <math>C</math> of a topological space <math>X</math> with <math>A \subseteq B \subseteq C \subseteq X</math> such that <math>A</math> is dense in <math>B</math> and <math>B</math> is dense in <math>C</math> (in the respective [[subspace topology]]) then <math>A</math> is also dense in <math>C.</math>

The [[Image (mathematics)|image]] of a dense subset under a [[Surjective function|surjective]] [[Continuous function (topology)|continuous]] function is again dense. The density of a topological space (the least of the [[Cardinality|cardinalities]] of its dense subsets) is a [[topological invariant]].

A topological space with a [[connected space|connected]] dense subset is necessarily connected itself.

Continuous functions into [[Hausdorff space]]s are determined by their values on dense subsets: if two continuous functions <math>f, g : X \to Y</math> into a [[Hausdorff space]] <math>Y</math> agree on a dense subset of <math>X</math> then they agree on all of <math>X.</math>

For metric spaces there are universal spaces, into which all spaces of given density can be [[Embedding|embedded]]: a metric space of density <math>\alpha</math> is isometric to a subspace of <math>C\left([0, 1]^{\alpha}, \R\right),</math> the space of real continuous functions on the [[Cartesian product#Infinite products|product]] of <math>\alpha</math> copies of the [[unit interval]].<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Kleiber|first1=Martin|last2=Pervin|first2=William J.|title=A generalized Banach-Mazur theorem|journal=Bull. Austral. Math. Soc.|date=1969|volume=1|issue=2|pages=169–173|doi=10.1017/S0004972700041411|doi-access=free}}</ref>

== Related notions ==

A point <math>x</math> of a subset <math>A</math> of a topological space <math>X</math> is called a [[limit point]] of <math>A</math> (in <math>X</math>) if every neighbourhood of <math>x</math> also contains a point of <math>A</math> other than <math>x</math> itself, and an [[isolated point]] of <math>A</math> otherwise. A subset without isolated points is said to be [[dense-in-itself]].

A subset <math>A</math> of a topological space <math>X</math> is called [[Nowhere dense set|nowhere dense]] (in <math>X</math>) if there is no neighborhood in <math>X</math> on which <math>A</math> is dense. Equivalently, a subset of a topological space is nowhere dense [[if and only if]] the interior of its closure is empty. The interior of the complement of a nowhere dense set is always dense. The complement of a closed nowhere dense set is a dense open set. Given a topological space <math>X,</math> a subset <math>A</math> of <math>X</math> that can be expressed as the union of countably many nowhere dense subsets of <math>X</math> is called [[Meagre set|meagre]]. The rational numbers, while dense in the real numbers, are meagre as a subset of the reals.

A topological space with a countable dense subset is called [[Separable space|separable]]. A topological space is a [[Baire space]] if and only if the intersection of countably many dense open sets is always dense. A topological space is called [[Resolvable space|resolvable]] if it is the union of two disjoint dense subsets. More generally, a topological space is called κ-resolvable for a [[Cardinal number|cardinal]] κ if it contains κ pairwise disjoint dense sets.

An [[embedding]] of a topological space <math>X</math> as a dense subset of a [[compact space]] is called a [[Compactification (mathematics)|compactification]] of <math>X.</math>

A [[linear operator]] between [[topological vector space]]s <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math> is said to be [[Densely defined operator|densely defined]] if its [[Domain of a function|domain]] is a dense subset of <math>X</math> and if its [[Image of a function|range]] is contained within <math>Y.</math> See also [[Continuous linear extension]].

A topological space <math>X</math> is [[Hyperconnected space|hyperconnected]] if and only if every nonempty open set is dense in <math>X.</math> A topological space is [[Submaximal space|submaximal]] if and only if every dense subset is open.

If <math>\left(X, d_X\right)</math> is a metric space, then a non-empty subset <math>Y</math> is said to be <math>\varepsilon</math>-dense if
<math display=block>\forall x \in X, \; \exists y \in Y \text{ such that } d_X(x, y) \leq \varepsilon.</math>

One can then show that <math>D</math> is dense in <math>\left(X, d_X\right)</math> if and only if it is ε-dense for every <math>\varepsilon > 0.</math>
